text:
Every recovery schedule I have reviewed had one thing in common: the end date did not move.

The project is three months late. A recovery schedule is requested. Two weeks later it arrives, and the completion date is exactly where it was in the baseline.

How? Almost always the same way:
• durations cut by 30 % with no change in crews or method
• activities that were sequential now run in parallel, on the same piece of steel
• productivity assumed at a rate the site has never achieved, not even for one week

On paper the gap is closed. On site, somebody has to close it, and that somebody is a person.

A recovery nobody resourced is paid for in 12-hour days, cancelled leave and weekends on site. The research says what that costs:
• 76 % of project professionals said their main project had caused them stress (APM survey of 1,000 practitioners).
• In construction, 24 % felt stressed every day of the past year, and 20 % reported constant fatigue, linked to long hours and high-pressure deadlines (CIOB, 2025).
• In the UAE, 84 % of employees reported stress, above the global average, and 48 % feel stressed most days at work (Cigna Healthcare, 2025; Mercer Marsh Benefits, 2025).
• Studies of construction project managers name time pressure as a main source of stress, and find that stress lowers their performance (Leung, Chan & Olomolaiye, 2008).

So the unrealistic schedule fails twice. It misses the date, and it wears out the people we need to finish the job.

A real recovery plan answers five questions:
1. What is different from now on: crews, shifts, sequence, method?
2. Can the site absorb it: supervision, access, permits, cranes?
3. What productivity does it need, and when did we last achieve it?
4. What does it ask of the people, and for how long?
5. If it still does not close the gap, what is the honest date?

Project managers and planners: when you sign a recovery schedule, who counts the hours it will take from your team? And what did the last "recovered" date really cost the people on your project?

#ProjectControls #Planning #Wellbeing #Construction #Leadership

The people who must deliver it: 76 % of project professionals stressed by their main project (APM, 1,000 surveyed); 24 % of construction workers stressed every day (CIOB, 2025); 84 % of UAE employees report stress (Cigna Healthcare, 2025). A real recovery also answers: what does it ask of the people, and for how long? And what is the honest date?
